title: Film buff brings community cinema back to town
content:
A film fan wants to restore cinema screenings to a town following the closure of a national chain in the area.
Will Preston, 28, is organising a community cinema event at Corn Market Hall in Kettering, Northamptonshire.
About 75 people are expected to attend a screening of The Rocky Horror Picture Show on 30 October.
Preston said: "We'd like to do [a screening] every month. We're moving around Kettering to all different places to try to keep it accessible and get as many people to enjoy the cinema experience as possible."
The Odeon in Kettering closed in January 2025 following what the building's owner, Augur Group, described as a "significant drop" in attendance over the past five years, making the venue "no longer viable".
Preston said he had fond memories of visiting the cinema with his parents and grandparents.
"It was a big part of the town and of who I am as a person," he said.
He began planning the community cinema in summer 2025 after a social media post attracted strong interest.
The response prompted him and his partner to research the equipment, licences and insurance needed to run screenings.
"We're going to keep it all as cheap as possible for people," he said.
"We're going to have tickets as cheap as possible, the snacks and stuff as cheap as possible, just to make it accessible."
In 2024, more than 2,000 people signed a petition to pledge their support for the Kettering Odeon and prevent its closure.
The cinema opened in 1997 with the James Bond film Tomorrow Never Dies, and its final screening was the Bob Dylan biopic, A Complete Unknown.

title: 'We put Middlesbrough on the map for dance music'
content:
The departing owners of one of Middlesbrough's most famous nightclubs say they put the town "on the map with dance music".
Father and son Barry Faulkner Sr and Barry Faulkner Jr are handing over the keys to The Middlesbrough Empire next month after 33 years in charge.
The Empire has hosted renowned DJs and acts including Pete Tong, the Arctic Monkeys and James Arthur, with Faulkner Jr saying he hoped the new owner would bring back some of the "glory days".
"At the time, I took a big chance with that place," Faulkner Sr said of taking the former bingo hall and turning it into a club, adding: "I think it cleared me out of money when I first got it."
He told BBC Radio Tees he was selling for health reasons, adding: "There's no use crying over spilt milk, you know what I mean? But it's our choice."
Faulkner Jr said they did not know what the new owners' intentions with the building were, but they were told it would close for about 18 months to "reinvent it".
The club said its events after 17 November would no longer take place at the Empire and would be relocated .
Faulkner Sr said the best night he had seen was when 2,000 people "crammed into the place" to see Paul Oakenfold.
"The place was just running with sweat," he said.
Meanwhile, Faulker Jr remembered people climbing on the roof and bonnet of the Bentley that brought DJ Sasha from Leeds to perform.
"You'd never seen anything like it," he said, adding: "Our life revolved around the Friday night.
"It was a family, we had a really good team."
The announcement sparked shock and sadness, with some saying the venue was their "second home" and their departure being the "end of an era".
Middlesbrough musician Finn Forster said headlining at the venue last year had been an "absolute dream" of his.
"Growing up, and seeing different artists from all over place come through and play Middlesbrough Empire, it shows you what's possible," Forster told BBC Radio Tees.
"I think, without it, there's a huge missing piece there."
He said the venue attracted "such a high calibre of artists".
Forster said: "It doesn't matter how small we are, or what we look like in comparison to the rest of the world, I think we can still have just as much of an important impact.
"And with the Empire, it's been a place that shines a light on the town as a place that can be trusted, whatever level of artist comes through."
Faulkner Sr and Faulkner Jr said they were looking forward to seeing "all the old faces" on their final night.

final_quality.reason: Significant local entertainment development, with notable achievements and comments from the departing owners and local musician Finn Forster, providing a clear reason for readers to care about the impact of the venue's closure on the community.

title: Original Traitors star became film actor after show
content:
A contestant from the first UK series of The Traitors has said the show transformed his life and helped launch his acting career.
Kieran Tompsett, 46, from Stevenage, Hertfordshire, was recruited as a traitor towards the end of the 2022 series, he was banished during the final episode, but memorably hinted at the identity of the last remaining traitor as he left.
Tompsett said the experience prompted him to ask: "What else do I want to do now?" He then decided to attend Ashley Walters' Kingdom Drama School.
He said: "I've trained for a year and a half and I've done three or four films now, I've done some supporting artist work to get some experience on set."
Earlier this year he appeared in the He-Man film Masters of the Universe, and will appear in an upcoming dark comedy called Damaged Goods.
Tompsett was working as a solutions consultant when he appeared on the hit BBC show in 2022 and now runs an AI workflow automation company.
He said: "I've just secured lead cast in a horror film for next year as well, so yeah, I'm going down a completely different path."
However, the former traitor admitted he initially found being in the public eye difficult.
He said: "I think in the first two years it was overwhelming. Anyone who has been on it will know you can't even go to Tesco and buy a meal deal at lunchtime without everyone staring at you.
"It's not a negative thing, but your privacy goes... I've always stopped and talked to everyone, still, it's quite hard to experience that loss of privacy, really."
